headline: High risk of prompt-injection and cascading errors from shared git/workspace plus Semantic Kernel MCP/plugin execution; data leakage and compliance risks are also material.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider reads and writes git-tracked files and shares state via a git repo, while Semantic Kernel can consume application context and invoke MCP/OpenAPI tools. That creates a plausible file-based injection path if Aider writes attacker-controlled content that B later treats as instructions. The pathway is not proven by docs alone, so I avoid high.
conditions: IF Aider writes untrusted text into repo files that Semantic Kernel later ingests as prompt/context, injection becomes active.
IF Semantic Kernel routes file-derived content into MCP or plugin calls without provenance checks, attacker instructions can propagate.
mitigations: Add a provenance tag to all repo-derived text before B ingests it.
Restrict B to read-only parsing of A's outputs for one test run.
Place A and B in separate repos or worktrees.
Disable MCP/plugin execution for any content sourced from A.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Aider touches source code and git history and has broad network egress; Semantic Kernel can send context to Azure OpenAI/OpenAI/Hugging Face/MCP servers. If they share a workspace, code or secrets written by A can flow into B's context and then out to third-party APIs. The shared-workspace assumption is plausible from A's shared git repo and B's application-defined files, but not fully documented, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or mounted workspace, B can ingest A's code and history.
IF B forwards that context to external model providers or MCP servers, sensitive code may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Run A and B on separate workspaces.
Remove secrets from the repo before either agent runs.
Disable external model providers for B during shared-workspace tests.
Use a redaction step on files before B reads them.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation at the orchestrator level.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider can write the filesystem and modify git state, while Semantic Kernel can also write files and call MCP/OpenAPI tools. In a shared repo or mutable workspace, both can race on the same artifacts without locking, and Aider's auto-commit behavior can conflict with B's writes. Because the profiles explicitly show overlapping write surfaces, the conflict is dangerous by default in shared-state setups.
conditions: IF both agents target the same git repository or directory, concurrent writes can overwrite each other.
IF B uses plugins that mutate shared files while Aider auto-commits, git history can diverge or be corrupted.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working tree.
Serialize write access with a simple lock file.
Pause B while Aider is committing.
Review and merge commits manually after each run.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency control in the orchestrator.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Aider produces code and git commits that Semantic Kernel can consume as application context, and B can then act through plugins or OpenAPI tools. If B treats A's output as authoritative, an error or hallucination in A can cascade into downstream actions or generated artifacts. The pair therefore has a default path from A's output to B's action-taking surface.
conditions: IF B uses Aider-generated code or commit messages as trusted context, errors can propagate.
IF B is configured to execute plugin actions based on that context, the cascade can affect external systems.
mitigations: Require B to verify A's outputs against tests or linting.
Block automatic execution of plugin actions from A-sourced text.
Use a human approval step before any external side effect.
Limit A to drafting only, not committing.
requires-engineering: add structured validation between A and B.

E_compliance.rationale: Aider handles source code, git history, and model-provider API keys, while Semantic Kernel handles application context and plugin credentials and may send context to Azure/OpenAI/Hugging Face or MCP servers. If regulated or secret-bearing data is placed in the shared workflow, retention and residency obligations can diverge across those providers. The profiles do not prove a specific jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable severity.
conditions: IF regulated data or secrets are present in the shared repo or context, provider retention policies become relevant.
IF B sends that context to external model providers without a DPA or residency controls, compliance gaps can arise.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace.
Disable external providers for B when sensitive data is present.
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately.
Document retention and residency settings for each provider.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data-class routing.
